articles.title: As Virat Kohli,  Rohit Sharma's era winds down, Lance Klusener sees Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as 'India’s next superstar'
articles.summary: Indian cricket has rarely struggled to find its next generation of stars, even when the players making way have seemed irreplaceable.
articles.body: Indian cricket has rarely struggled to find its next generation of stars, even when the players making way have seemed irreplaceable. From Sunil Gavaskar to Sachin Tendulkar, and from Tendulkar to Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma, every era has brought its own icons, with fresh talent eventually stepping into the spotlight.As Indian cricket prepares for life beyond Kohli and Rohit, former South African all-rounder Lance Klusener believes the transition need not be a difficult one. He has backed Shubman Gill to lead India for years to come while identifying teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as a potential superstar of the future.Speaking to IANS, he pointed to cricket's history of producing players who challenge records once considered untouchable.‘Cricket carries on’: Klusener on life after Kohli and Rohit“As good as Virat and as good as Rohit have been in the past, they will have to walk away from the game when their time comes. But the beauty of cricket is that it carries on. It gets stronger sometimes.“When we played, people never thought that Sachin Tendulkar’s records would ever be broken. And people are challenging those already. So, players come and go. It’s a sad day when legends of your game and legends of your country step away. But on the bright side, there are always younger, fitter, faster players in the wings as well,” Klusener told IANS.The comparison with Tendulkar is particularly relevant. His records once appeared beyond reach, yet subsequent generations have continued to raise the bar, reinforcing Klusener's belief that Indian cricket has enough depth to sustain its success even as two of its defining modern-day figures approach the end of their international careers.Shubman Gill and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi represent India's next generationKlusener's confidence in India's future rests on the emergence of young players capable of shouldering greater responsibility. Gill, who has already taken on leadership responsibilities across formats, is viewed as a central figure in India's long-term plans.“For me personally, I’m convinced already. I think he’s the right man for the job. He’s an absolute superstar with the bat. It’s probably just being able to separate Shubman Gill as a batter and Shubman Gill as a captain as well. I think all the great captains have been able to separate that. And I’m sure he’ll have a lot of opportunities and a lot of people to lean on in helping him do that,'' Lance said on Gill.He pointed to Sooryavanshi as evidence that another generation of Indian talent is already emerging.“But cricket goes on. Stars come and go, and legends retire, and people think that it’ll never be the same again. But India doesn’t have to look further than a youngster like Sooryavanshi. There’s the next superstar,” he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: South Africa meet Australia in third Test series-decider at Cape Town with careers on the line for tourists
articles.summary: Australia's Marnus Labuschagne may have one innings to save his skin as poor run continues in South Africa; Steve Smith faces late fitness test; series locked at 1-1 after South Africa's innings victory in Gqeberha; watch live on Sky Sports Cricket from 7.30am, Tuesday
articles.body:
Should they lose to South Africa this week in the series decider, live on Sky Sports Cricket , a number of careers could be ended.

Having been humbled by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha last time out, a game in which they were torpedoed for 99 in the first innings, the Baggy Greens need a response.

If that does not come, the reaction from the Australian media could be more abrasive than the piece of sandpaper Cameron Bancroft aimed to conceal down his trousers eight years ago.

The batting has been creaking for a while.

In the 4-1 Ashes thrashing of England last winter, it was held together by Travis Head, Steve Smith and Alex Carey as others toiled, while in South Africa so far the tourists have managed only three individual fifty-plus scores - one for Head and two for Matt Renshaw.

Without Head in Durban, things would have been even grislier. His second-innings 121 was 81 more runs than the next highest score by an Aussie in the game.

Even the great Smith - who received a ban for the role he played as skipper in 'Sandpapergate' in 2018, along with Bancroft and David Warner - has stuttered: three innings' in the 20s and a knock of three.

He was hampered by a neck problem in Gqeberha and faces a late fitness Test ahead of the winner-takes-all Cape Town finale.

If he fails that, it could aid Marnus Labuschagne's hopes of staying in the side.

Labuschagne and selector Bailey under big pressure?

Former Australia captain Ricky Ponting had branded Labuschagne's spot as "untenable" after a lean return at home to Bangladesh left him without a Test century in 43 innings, stretching back to the 2023 Ashes in England. That has now extended to 47 innings.

Labuschagne has had no trouble starting in South Africa, the country of his birth - reaching the 30s in three of his four outings. But he has not kicked on.

Pinned lbw. Sliced loosely to cover. Brilliantly caught by Simon Harmer at gully. And then a criminal dismissal as he inexplicably holed out to long-on in the second innings of the second Test, a game Australia were trying to save.

If he misses out this week, it could be curtains. If he plays and fails, it could be a similar story. If Australia fail as a team, perhaps pressure will mount on head selector George Bailey?

Former skipper Steve Waugh said before the Ashes that Bailey has previously shown a lack of "appetite" to make the big calls, while the selection of the now-jettisoned Nic Maddinson for the South Africa tour was panned at the time by Matthew Hayden.

Maddinson ditching after recall highlights Australia's issues

Maddinson, 34, had not played a first-class game since March 2025 due to a testicular cancer diagnosis and averaged 6.75 from his first three Tests back in 2016.

Hayden accused selectors of "disrespecting first-class cricket" and "promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we've seen in a generation of cricket."

Maddinson has not been as good as mediocre in this series, with his average a paltry 14 after amassing only 56 runs from four knocks - 48 of which came in one innings to punctuate a 33-ball duck, a four-ball duck and a 10-ball eight.

He has since been released from the squad, with Renshaw poised to open alongside Head in Cape Town.

Considering what he went through health-wise, people were rooting for Maddinson to perform but he hasn't. It raises the question over whether a younger player should have been given a go instead.

Ollie Davies, Sam Konstas and Campbell Kellaway were options. Nathan McSweeney, too.

The problem Australia have is that unlike in previous eras when they had players averaging north of 40 and banging out domestic runs - often in English county cricket as well as at home - waiting in the wings, they don't now.

All of the prospects mentioned above average mid-30s or lower in first-class cricket.

Will Bavuma extend excellent record as captain?

South Africa, by contrast, have a pretty much guaranteed source of runs in captain Temba Bavuma, whose brilliant 179 from 334 balls in Gqeberha means he is averaging 49.95 across his last 28 Tests.

His nuggety ton last time out was scored after he came in at 12-2.

He was at the other end as the Proteas slumped to 110-6 before pushing them to 425-9 and was ultimately left to celebrate a 12th win in 14 Tests as skipper.

This feels like a great chance to make that 13 from 15 unless Australia are able to pull something out of the bag in Cape Town.

Unlike in 2018, something within the rules this time.

articles.title: Gareth Batty: Surrey head coach leaves to join IPL side Chennai Super Kings
articles.summary: Surrey head coach Gareth Batty steps down to join Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings as assistant head coach.
articles.body:
Surrey head coach Gareth Batty has stepped down to join Indian Premier League side Chennai Super Kings as an assistant coach.

Batty led Surrey to three consecutive County Championship titles in his first three seasons in charge and twice guided them to T20 Finals Day.

"Thank you hardly seems enough for all that Surrey has meant to me," the former England spinner told the club's website , external .

"The new journey is a very exciting one for my family and I, and I'm looking forward to getting going."

Batty's departure ends a 21-year association with Surrey.

He had two spells as a player, the first from 1998 to 2001 after leaving Yorkshire. He then spent seven seasons at Worcestershire before returning to The Oval in 2010.

Batty was club captain between 2015 and 2017, and in total played more than 350 times for Surrey, taking more than 500 wickets across all formats.

Batty, who played nine Tests for England, retired in 2021 and immediately joined Surrey's coaching staff.

After he was appointed head coach in 2022 , Surrey became the first team in nearly 60 years to win three County Championship titles in a row.

"It is difficult to put into words just how much Gareth Batty has given to Surrey County Cricket Club, both as a player and as head coach," director of cricket Alec Stewart said.

"I have known and worked with Gareth for many years and throughout that time he has shown an outstanding commitment to this club.

"While we are sorry to see him go, I understand that this opportunity was too good for him to pass up on and will enable him to spend more time with his family outside of the IPL season."

Three of the 10 teams who will play in Division One of the County Championship next season are now without a head coach, after Glamorgan's Richard Dawson joined the England set-up and newly-promoted Durham's Ryan Campbell moved upstairs to become the club's director of cricket.

articles.title: 'Is this the first time there's chaos?': Phil Simmons responds after Bangladesh remove batting coach Mohammad Ashraful
articles.summary: Bangladesh head coach Phil Simmons has sought to keep the focus firmly on the field amid questions over the team's preparations following the removal of
articles.body: Bangladesh head coach Phil Simmons has sought to keep the focus firmly on the field amid questions over the team's preparations following the removal of batting coach Mohammad Ashraful, insisting that the squad remains united and determined to make the most of its World Test Championship (WTC) campaign.With a two-Test series against West Indies beginning in Mirpur on Wednesday, Bangladesh will be keen to put a turbulent period behind them and strengthen their position in the WTC standings. The team currently sits fourth in the table, making the home series an important opportunity to collect valuable points in the race for a place in the final.The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) announced on Saturday that Ashraful had been reassigned from his role as batting coach, with Mohammad Salahuddin taking over on an interim basis. The decision came after a mixed run of results in the UAE, where Bangladesh drew a one-off Test against Afghanistan before losing both their matches in the ODI tri-series involving Afghanistan and Zimbabwe.The coaching change prompted speculation about unrest within the setup and whether recent results had influenced the board's decision. Simmons, however, played down the suggestion that the developments had unsettled his players, stressing that their attention was on preparation and the challenge ahead.‘Is this the first time there's chaos before a match?’: Simmons“Is this the first time there's chaos before a match?” Simmons said ahead of the first Test, according to cricinfo.“Every series is important. Those that we played earlier in the year were important too. But the thing is how we go about our preparation for the series. I think that the group that was here have been excellent in the last three or four days. They've been doing their work and now the whole team joins together. It's what we do over the next two days, it's not what's happening outside, it's what we do as a team to prepare,” he added.Simmons also highlighted the significance of the WTC campaign, pointing to the opportunity Bangladesh have to compete for a place in the championship final.“I think everyone is very focused on the Test match. The same in the Test match in Abu Dhabi, I think everyone was focused on the Test match and what's in front of them. I think there's that goal and that desire to play in the World Test Championship and this is the first time we've had that opportunity to be there. So I think everyone is going to be up and ready for the Test matches,” he said.Simmons defends Bangladesh's approach in Afghanistan TestBangladesh's drawn Test against Afghanistan in Abu Dhabi earlier this month attracted criticism, with questions raised over the batting approach and whether the team had done enough to force a result. Simmons defended the players, arguing that they had followed the intended strategy and that the pitch had become more favourable for batting than the team had anticipated on the final day.“I don't think it was a case where they didn't respond to the match situation. I think that they played it exactly how we wanted to play it. The wicket got better than we thought. So on the last day, it was a lot better than we thought it would be on the last day,” he said.The coach also pointed to missed opportunities in the field, including a missed run-out chance and dropped catches, which he felt had cost Bangladesh the opportunity to secure victory.“I think from that, at the end of the day, we should have won the Test match. We missed a run-out, we dropped a few catches. So, at the end of the day, we should have won the match, but I don't think we played it in the wrong way,” Simmons added.Bangladesh vs West Indies: Test series scheduleThe first Test will be played at the Shere Bangla National Stadium in Mirpur from October 28, while the second Test is scheduled to begin in Sylhet on November 5.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Karnataka recover from slow start to bowl out Tripura for 194, Shikhar Shetty takes five
articles.summary: MYSURU: There was no early morning rush from Karnataka’s bowlers, nor a concerted effort to exploit the movement on offer in the first hour.
articles.body: MYSURU: There was no early morning rush from Karnataka’s bowlers, nor a concerted effort to exploit the movement on offer in the first hour. The decision to go in with three spinners and two pacers against Tripura looked questionable, and every move seemed open to second-guessing. But Karnataka eventually found their rhythm on the opening day of their Group B league fixture at the SDNRW Ground here, helped in no small measure by the visitors’ self-inflicted damage.Left-arm spinner Shikhar Shetty led the turnaround with a five-wicket haul (5/54) as Karnataka bowled out Tripura for 194 with medium pacer Manvanth Kumar returning 3 for 23.However, the hosts were left with a familiar problem to contend with in the final over of the day. Opener Mayank Agarwal fell to hard hands, jabbing Abhijith Sarkar to Sridam Paul at second slip. Karnataka ended the day at 10/1, with Rohan Patil and Vyshak Vijaykumar at the crease.Earlier, after opting to bowl, Karnataka failed to make much headway with the new ball. There was little emphasis on bowling at the stumps. While the plan was to make the batters play, Vyshak strayed down the leg side too often, even as he employed three slips and a gully. The introduction of spin in the seventh over did little to change the script, with Tripura adopting a defensive approach to negotiate the first hour.Manvanth Kumar, who bowled a good length, provided the breakthrough when Hrituraj Roy miscued a drive to wicketkeeper KL Shrijith. Babul Dey followed, edging a delivery from Manvanth that pitched outside off to Shrijith. At the other end, Bikramkumar Das (53) kept the scoreboard moving as Tripura reached 88/2 at lunch.A well-set Das fell in the first over after the break, chasing a delivery from Vyshak that moved away and edging it to Karun Nair in the slips.That was the opening Karnataka needed, as Tripura's middle order began to unravel. Shreyas Gopal accounted for Sridam Paul, who went on the back foot against a short ball and offered a catch to KV Aneesh at first slip. Dangerman Mandeep Singh then stepped out against Shikhar, only to find Manvanth at mid-off.Skipper M Murasingh, fresh from a century in the previous match, struck a few boundaries before being undone by a Shikhar yorker that crashed into his stumps.Sentu Sarkar (12), Bikram Debnath (33 not out) and Parvez Sultan offered some resistance through a defensive approach. But Manvanth dismissed Sentu before Shikhar removed Sultan, who swept the spinner only to be caught by Manvanth at fine leg.Shikhar then needed little time to clean up the tail and register his third five-wicket haul in first-class cricket.Explaining the decision to field a spin-heavy attack, which meant leaving out pacers Vidwath Kaverappa and Abhilash Shetty, head coach R Vinay Kumar said: “The wicket is quite dry, so we thought of going with three spinners and two seamers. articles.title: 'Stand near a powerful fan': India coach's unique advice to players ahead of Wellington Test
articles.summary: The wind at Wellington's Basin Reserve can change direction without warning, making it a challenging venue for visiting teams.
articles.body: The wind at Wellington's Basin Reserve can change direction without warning, making it a challenging venue for visiting teams. India's bowling coach Morne Morkel has offered a simple piece of advice to the Test specialists yet to arrive in New Zealand: prepare to deal with the strong winds before stepping onto the field.India will play a two-match Test series against New Zealand after the ongoing T20I and ODI series. The first Test is scheduled to begin at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on November 18.Morkel's advice to the players is to "Stand near a powerful fan to counter the speedy wind", which has troubled visiting teams at the venue for years."We've spoken about Wellington, especially before the start of the tour, and we've planted those seeds. I spoke to some of the boys who were back in India last night, and they asked what the conditions are like. I said, 'Make sure you get a very strong fan at home. When you walk into the fan that is going to be your preparation'," Morkel said ahead of India's third T20 International.The Indian team is currently in Wellington, New Zealand's capital, which is also known as "Windy Wellington". Wind speeds reached 120 kmph on Monday.Although the third T20I against the Black Caps is scheduled for Tuesday, Morkel and head coach Gautam Gambhir are already looking ahead to the challenges the team could face in the Test series."This wind is a different beast. I was in the hotel this morning and the whole building was sort of shaking. So I think it's going to be a new sort of thing that we add to our books for the guys to get used to and accustomed to with a quick turnaround," Morkel said.He added that India would need to face the conditions without making excuses, as the wind could affect several aspects of the game, including a batter's stance and position at the crease."For us, it is looking forward to that challenge and taking it head-on and not really making excuses. This wind can impact a lot of things, it can impact batting, your stance, your crease, it can impact many factors," Morkel said.The former South Africa fast bowler has experienced the conditions at the Basin Reserve during his playing career. He said adjusting to the wind in just a few days of training was difficult, making it important for players to approach the challenge with the right mindset."When I toured here with South Africa, we had certain ways that we went about trying to get used to it. I don't think you can ever get used to it in the space of two, three, or four days. So it comes down to how you're going to frame the whole situation: you're either going to see it as a challenge, or you're going to see it as a negative and let it down."Hopefully, we can get those guys in a mental space where they look forward to that challenge. At the end of the day, you need somebody to put their hand up and bowl into the wind, because we can't have four guys bowling off the wind."New Zealand all-rounder Michael Bracewell is also aware of the problems the conditions can create for visiting teams. He said the hosts would look to make the most of any discomfort their opponents experience.Bracewell pointed out that wind behaves differently at enclosed stadiums, where it can swirl and change direction, compared with more open grounds such as the Basin Reserve."It is interesting. At closed stadiums, it swirls around a bit, so it's probably not as consistent as it is when you play in a slightly more open field like the Basin. We had one game here where the cameras got turned off from one end because it was so windy," Bracewell said.However, he also sees dealing with different conditions as an important part of international cricket, where teams must adapt to the challenges they encounter around the world."So that's the joy of playing here is you get faced with different conditions, and that's the great thing about international cricket. You go all around the world and have to deal with different things."So it swirls a bit in the stadium, so it's not necessarily that there's going to be one end that perhaps if we're playing in an open sort of stadium that you could target.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: In-form Ward eyeing further Jersey progress
articles.summary: Ben Ward hopes Jersey can win their remaining ICC Challenge League A matches in preparation for the next stage of World Cup qualification.
articles.body:
Ben Ward hopes Jersey can win their remaining ICC Challenge League A matches as preparation for the next stage of World Cup qualification.

Leg spinner Ward has taken five wickets in each of Jersey's two matches in the final round of Challenge League games in Kenya.

He had figures of 5-49 in the win over Papua New Guinea before taking 5-28 against the hosts on Sunday.

The wins secured Jersey the Challenge League A title and a place in the ICC Cricket World Cup Qualifier play-off in Nepal in December - the second of three qualifying stages for the 2027 Cricket World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

"I think going unbeaten is something that you as a cricketer will always want," Ward told BBC Jersey.

"It's not always going to happen the way that you want it, but I think that is our goal.

"More so our goal is the big picture - play these games with good intensity, tournament intensity, and maybe even try out a few new things, a few new tactics that may work on a larger scale.

"Playing against better opposition we'll have to probably be more tactically aware than relying solely on our skills, so it's going to be a good learning experience and these three games coming up are against strong opposition, so if we continue playing the way we can and implementing new skills, then it's even more exciting."

Jersey still have to play Kuwait, Denmark and Qatar in Nairobi as they plot a return to the second stage of qualifying for the Cricket World Cup, having reached the same stage three years ago.

It comes as Jersey's global stock continues to rise - they missed out on a place at this year's T20 World Cup on net run rate having beaten Scotland and narrowly lost to the Netherlands in the final round of European qualifying.

"It will be a step up, but we've got a good bunch of guys, we've got some strong, strong players and most importantly we're a real team unit, we're all mates," added Ward, who plays his club cricket in South Africa for Cape Town-based Durbanville.

"We get on well, we know when someone's not at their best and we help lift them up again.

"These teams that play at that higher level are obviously professionals, they've got contracts, they do that as their main job, where most of us are working other jobs.

"But what we have is that unity of growing up playing cricket together and knowing each other inside and out.

"We're ready for it and we've played some serious cricket in this and hopefully we can move that forward."

In the meantime, Ward is focused on continuing to help his native island out in Nairobi.

Jersey have lost just one of their 12 ICC Challenge League matches - the six-team round-robin event sees sides come together once a year for three years to play each other, with the top two progressing to the next stage of Cricket World Cup qualification.

And while Jersey's batters have impressed - Zak Tribe has hit 215 runs while his brother, Glamorgan batter Asa, has chipped in with 95 - Ward has been the pick of Jersey's bowling attack.

"It's been coming out of the hand quite nicely to say the least," he added.

"I've definitely bowled better for less and I've definitely bowled worse for more, maybe not five-fers in a row, that's almost unheard of in some aspects, but I'm very, very happy with where my cricket is at the moment.

"It's not just one person - I may have got five wickets in this game, but our batters put on an unbelievable score, our other bowlers put on a lot of pressure, and to have Jake Dunford behind the stumps the way he is, he's an unbelievable wicketkeeper.

"For me, at the top of my mark, I feel like if I get anywhere near the batter's bat or if they even think about leaving their crease, they've got no chance with him behind the stumps.

"So it's a good little team within a team that we have there, but for me personally, it feels like it's coming out quite well and we'll see how it goes - you can only play what's in front of you."

articles.title: 'Last peice of puzzle': Pat Cummins reveals Australia’s plan for Steve Smith after neck injury ahead of South Africa decider
articles.summary: Australia captain Pat Cummins is keeping his fingers crossed over Steve Smith’s availability for the third and final Test against South Africa, with the
articles.body: Australia captain Pat Cummins is keeping his fingers crossed over Steve Smith’s availability for the third and final Test against South Africa, with the visitors prepared to give their experienced batter as much time as possible to prove his fitness ahead of the series decider in Cape Town.Smith sustained a neck injury during Australia’s innings-and-31-run defeat in the second Test at Gqeberha, which levelled the three-match series at 1-1. With the decisive contest at Newlands beginning on Tuesday, Australia are reluctant to make a final call on Smith until they have a clearer picture of his condition.“Hopefully, it all goes well and he'll be there,” Cummins told reporters on Monday. “But we just want to wait for that last piece of the puzzle before naming a team.”Smith’s fitness is a key concern for Australia as they look to respond to their heavy defeat in the second Test and reclaim the advantage in the series. The batter has endured a challenging tour with the bat, averaging a little over 20 across four innings, and had also taken a blow to the head during the opening Test.Cummins backs Smith amid fitness concernsCummins was full of praise for Smith’s approach throughout the tour, highlighting his involvement with the team and the positive mindset he has brought to the dressing room.“He's been awesome this tour,” Cummins said. “In the last couple of years, probably particularly the last 12 months, it feels like he's in a really good place and he's enjoying his cricket.”The Australia captain added that Smith has remained engaged with the group away from the field, whether through playing golf or his regular morning coffee outings, and has continued to provide support to the team.“He's been super invested in what's going on and very helpful for me out in the middle,” Cummins said.The Australian skipper also underlined Smith’s stature in the game, pointing out that even the finest batters have to contend with injuries and physical setbacks over the course of long international careers.“He looks in total control of how he's going about his work. He's one of the greatest batters we've ever had. You don't play 100-odd Tests without matches where you're not 100% fit,” Cummins added.Cameron Green set for middle-order role as Australia weigh optionsCummins indicated that Cameron Green would preferably bat in the middle order, a decision that could see Matt Renshaw open alongside Travis Head. The possibility has gained traction after Nic Maddinson was dropped from the squad. articles.summary: Five-time IPL champions Chennai Super Kings (CSK) have begun a major overhaul of their support staff ahead of the 2027 season, parting ways with several
articles.body: Five-time IPL champions Chennai Super Kings (CSK) have begun a major overhaul of their support staff ahead of the 2027 season, parting ways with several long-serving members, including batting coach Mike Hussey and bowling coach Eric Simons. The changes come weeks after the franchise appointed former India pacer Zaheer Khan as head coach, replacing Stephen Fleming.Hussey, who joined CSK as batting coach in 2018 after playing six seasons for the franchise, will not continue in the role from IPL 2027.“From the very first season in 2008, you have been an integral part of the Chennai Super Kings family,” CSK said on their social media handles while announcing the decision to part ways with Hussey.“Your journey in Yellow has been defined not just by the runs you scored and the players you mentored, but by the dedication, humility, and unwavering commitment you brought to this franchise over the years.“Your place in our history will forever remain special, Hussmeister. Once a Super King, always a Super King,” the statement read.The Super Kings have also officially announced their decision to part ways with bowling coach Eric Simons. As reported earlier by TimesofIndia.com, former India pacer Mohit Sharma is set to join Zaheer's support staff as the new bowling coach.Assistant coach Rajiv Kumar and fielding coach James Foster will also leave the backroom staff ahead of the 2027 season.The franchise has further decided not to retain physio Tommy Simsek and strength and conditioning coach Gregory King.Meanwhile, former England spinner Gareth Batty has joined CSK as an assistant coach. Batty, 49, played nine Tests, 10 ODIs and one T20I for England. He is familiar with Zaheer, having worked with him during their time at English county Worcestershire.CSK's changes come after three seasons in which the franchise failed to match its past success. Since winning the IPL title in 2023, the team has finished fifth in 2024, 10th in 2025 and eighth in 2026.The team's performances led to the end of its long association with Fleming, who has since taken charge of England's Test team. articles.title: Nitish Kumar Reddy strengthens his case as India's next pace-bowling allrounder
articles.summary: That Nitish Kumar Reddy, being one of only two players named in all three squads for the New Zealand tour, speaks volumes about how highly India rate his
articles.body: That Nitish Kumar Reddy, being one of only two players named in all three squads for the New Zealand tour, speaks volumes about how highly India rate his skills.It has also provided the team management with an opportunity to develop an alternative to the often-injured Hardik Pandya, who is not getting any younger. On his part, the 25-year-old has made useful contributions to justify the faith shown in him.Reddy bowled his full quota of four overs in the first T20I in Christchurch and was entrusted with the responsibility of delivering the 19th over. He conceded 12 runs in that over and finished with a joint-best economy rate of 10, alongside Mayank Yadav.In the second game, he was once again handed the ball in the 19th over. This time, he conceded just 14 runs and claimed a wicket. The right-hander later returned to stitch together an unbeaten 69-run partnership off 30 balls with Tilak Varma to steer India to victory from a difficult position. He finished unbeaten on 26 off 13 balls.Those two performances are a testament to his ever-improving skills as an allrounder. The team think tank has recognised his potential and has preferred him over Shivam Dube since the third T20I against the West Indies. While he cannot yet be put in the same league as Pandya, whose skill set remains superior to that of any other Indian allrounder, Reddy has age on his side and continues to improve both aspects of his game, besides being an excellent fielder.India bowling coach Morne Morkel believes Reddy has the skills to become the all-format allrounder India have been desperately searching for and one who could eventually emerge as Pandya's successor.Morkel recently backed him publicly, stating that he is a player to "keep an eye on" and someone capable of producing a "magical ball" to unsettle batters.Reddy, too, does not shy away from questions about his credentials as an allrounder, nor does he shy away from putting in hard yards."The amount of work I have to do is more than anyone else, on and off the field," he said after the second game against New Zealand.Reddy made his Test debut during the 2024 tour of Australia and gave a good account of himself, including a century at the MCG against a bowling attack featuring Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon.While he showed what he could do with the bat, his bowling lacked the much-needed zip required to cement a regular place in the XI as an allrounder. He addressed that shortcoming by working with Steffan Jones, a former county cricketer and now a fast-bowling and high-performance coach, shortly before the 2026 IPL.The results were there for everyone to see. His pace consistently touched the mid-130kph range, a significant improvement from the mid-120s he had been bowling before his sessions with Jones.Reddy's biggest challenge, however, remains his fitness. He was set to travel to Zimbabwe for his maiden India call-up after the 2024 T20 World Cup, but a hernia injury scuppered those plans. Since then, he has spent considerable time on the sidelines with various injuries, including a freak gym accident in which he injured his left knee. Earlier this year, a quadriceps injury also ruled him out of the UK tour.With Reddy improving with every outing, the onus is now on the team management to use him judiciously and keep him fit and ready for the bigger challenges that lie ahead.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: James Anderson: Lancashire to look into farewell for legendary bowler amid fan anger
articles.summary: Lancashire will look into organising a farewell for bowler James Anderson amid fan unrest over his departure from the club.
articles.body:
Lancashire will look into organising a farewell for bowler James Anderson amid fan unrest over his departure from the club.

It was announced last week the 44-year-old, England's all-time leading wicket-taker, has been released by the county he first represented in 2001.

The topic dominated a tense meeting between the club hierarchy and members at Old Trafford on Monday evening, with many members angered by the decision.

Some raised their upset at the fact the end-of-season decision had denied fans the chance to thank Anderson for his service to the county and celebrate his career.

The club, represented by new chief executive Richard Kenyon and incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace, agreed to look into a solution.

Farbrace joined the meeting via video from his holiday in the United States and is understood to have taken ownership of the decision when taking questions from members.

The former England assistant coach, who left his role in charge of Sussex before joining the Red Rose county, reiterated his explanation from Lancashire's public statement on Sunday - that he wants to build a squad capable of winning the County Championship within the next four years and does not believe Anderson, who turns 45 next year, will play a part in that.

One attendee among about 200 members at the meeting told BBC Sport the atmosphere in the room remained mixed.

Other members suggested Farbrace had gone some way to calming the unrest.

Anderson was Lancashire's captain in the County Championship last season and while the county finished second bottom in Division Two, continuing a poor run of results in recent years, he remained one of their best performers.

He took 50 wickets and was named their Championship player of the year.

A number of counties have expressed an interest in signing the veteran for next season.

Anderson first played List A cricket in 2000 as a 17-year-old for the Lancashire Cricket Board against Suffolk.

He made his professional debut for Lancashire a year later and was in the England team by the end of 2002.

In addition to his 911 international wickets - an England record and a record for all pace bowlers - Anderson claimed 443 first-class scalps for Lancashire, along with 83 in List A cricket and a further 50 in T20s.

When his England career was abruptly ended in 2024, Anderson opted to continue playing with Lancashire in 2025.

At the time, he said he felt he could play for three more years.

In his first public comment since the decision on Sunday, he expressed his sadness at the situation but stopped short of retiring.

articles.title: 'Not trying to reinvent the wheel': Luke Williams backs Mumbai Indians' core for WPL 2027 | EXCLUSIVE
articles.summary: Mumbai Indians missed the Women’s Premier League playoffs last season after injuries and illness disrupted their combinations and close games slipped away.
articles.body: Mumbai Indians missed the Women’s Premier League playoffs last season after injuries and illness disrupted their combinations and close games slipped away. New head coach Luke Williams believes the franchise can return to contention without making wholesale changes to a side that has won two titles in four seasons.“Certainly not trying to reinvent the wheel,” Williams told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction from Adelaide.The Australian takes over from Lisa Keightley, who left after one season in charge. Keightley had succeeded Charlotte Edwards, who guided Mumbai to their inaugural WPL title in 2023. Williams knows Edwards from their time working in England’s women’s setup and arrives with a WPL title of his own, having coached Royal Challengers Bengaluru to the championship in 2024.He spent the 2026 season away from the competition, but when the Mumbai job became available, the prospect of returning to WPL - and working with Harmanpreet Kaur - appealed to him.“I was sort of, I guess, still a little bit surprised when it came about,” he said. “And from my end, I was extremely honoured and was interested straight away. Obviously, I've had some previous experience in the WPL. I had a year away from it last season and really missed being involved in the competition.”Mumbai are the two-time WPL winners, and Williams said the franchise’s record, along with the prospect of responding to a difficult campaign, made the role attractive.“The success that MI have had in all leagues, but also the WPL with two titles in the four years, was really exciting. And probably coming off a tougher year last year as well is a motivating factor to try and bounce back straight away and really compete for the title this year,” he said.Injuries, close games and the need for consistencyMumbai finished the 2026 league stage with three wins and five defeats, with Hayley Matthews missing the first three matches with a quad injury, while Nat Sciver-Brunt also dealt with illness. Harmanpreet scored 342 runs, Sciver-Brunt made 321, and Amelia Kerr took 14 wickets, but Mumbai could not convert enough individual performances into wins.Williams pointed to the difficulty of settling combinations in a tournament with only eight league matches. Mumbai lost close games, including their opening fixture against RCB, and had little time to recover from setbacks.“It looked like a challenging year with some injury and illness at different times. So trying to settle the combination down at different times is a big part of it. There were some close games, even the first game of the tournament against RCB. I think in this tournament where there's only eight games, close games are so important to try to get them to go in your direction. And try to win those crucial moments,” he said.“Still had a positive net run rate last year, I think. Mumbai and RCB were the only two teams to finish with a positive net run rate. So there's still a lot of positive signs. But just a couple of areas that we can hopefully have a bit of fortune with injury and illness. But also make sure that our processes, especially in the tighter games, are really clear and able to get over the line in those.”Williams does not intend to overhaul the team’s approach. He wants players to be clear about their responsibilities, while allowing for changes as their games develop between WPL seasons.“Primarily there's a lot to continue on with, I think, in terms of philosophy. But again, I guess [with] each player, it's a year between WPLs. So the players would have developed different things. So being really clear on their role within the side, where there might be some subtle shifts from different years with that,” he said.He pointed to the retentions as an indication of the franchise’s plans.“But again, in terms of the overall makeup, I think, or the composition, you could probably see from our retentions that we're keen to retain that core nucleus of the squad. But again, there may be some subtle changes to different roles and how we go about little bits and pieces. But certainly not trying to reinvent the wheel.”Harmanpreet stays on as captainHarmanpreet will continue to lead Mumbai, even as her international captaincy has ended. She stepped down as India captain this month, having led the team to its first Women’s Cricket World Cup title in 2025.For Williams, Harmanpreet remains central to his plans at Mumbai. The two have spoken online and over the phone and met during his recent visit to India.“Harman is obviously such an integral part of MI as well as Indian cricket, obviously. And will continue in the captaincy role and has just a huge presence within the franchise. Is really strong with her thoughts and beliefs and we're really aligned in how we want to take the team forward for not only this year but hopefully years to come,” Williams said.He values her ability to combine an intense competitive streak with composure when making decisions under pressure.“She's able to, I think, mix a steely sort of competitiveness and desire and all those attributes that you want to see in a leader, with still having a calmness and a game knowledge and an ability to make really good decisions under pressure,” he said.“So I love the combination of the leader that's there and stands up and always wants to compete, but also at the same time is able to be really calculated in the decisions that they make.”The auction: immediate needs and future optionsThe WPL auction takes place in Kochi on October 28. Mumbai have retained Harmanpreet, Matthews, Sciver-Brunt and Kerr among others, giving Williams an experienced core to build around.His priority is to find players whose strengths complement those already in the squad, while ensuring the team has options for different pitches and conditions.“It's making sure that each person has some strengths that we feel can, I guess, be accentuated in our program, that will match well with other players that we've got, I guess, depending on the conditions that we're playing in, we've got options for wickets, whether they're turning wickets or slow wickets or whatever conditions we face, we've got a number of options to be able to do that,” he said.The search will not be limited to players expected to start every game. Williams also wants signings who can put pressure on the first-choice XI and step in when needed.“So we're in a really good position, I think, with a strong nucleus, experienced nucleus, but I think that's probably the primary function of the upcoming auction is to really be targeted in some players that we think can add, whether that's in the starting XI or putting pressure on or be ready to go if an opportunity presents,” he said.With the current WPL auction cycle entering its final year, immediate contribution will carry weight in recruitment. Williams said the franchise would nevertheless consider younger players who could remain part of the squad beyond the coming season.“Primarily in the last year of a cycle, you probably do lean towards immediate outputs and what the person can do in the next 12 months. That's probably certainly the initial lens that you look at players through,” he said.“But again, having a look at young players that may be able to be part of the franchise for a longer period of time, certainly cast an eye over that and be aware of that. And depending on how the auction goes or the person and how it unfolds, we're certainly open to that option as well to add to our list.”Data has its place, but players need to trust their gameWilliams has coached in the WPL and Australia’s Women’s Big Bash League, worked with England’s women’s team and been part of a title-winning Southern Brave staff in The Hundred. Across those environments, he said, preparation and confidence in individual roles remain central.“A lot of the same things are about making sure that your teams are as well-prepared as they possibly can be, that they're really confident in their own roles and also their teammates and the style of play that you want to do and really trying to get an environment that's happy and people are really enjoying themselves,” he said.“There's some ups and downs in T20 cricket. So, having a group that's really supportive of each other, that understands that there will be those ups and downs and are able to bounce back quickly after a tough game or a tough over or a tough delivery at different times is so important.”He likes using data and analytics, but does not believe every player needs to be thinking about match-ups and statistics while batting or bowling. The information has to suit the individual.“There's certain players that obviously the actual data or which bowlers potentially to target or batters to target or different fields really works for them. That's a bit of information. For others, I think it needs to very much be in the background, and the clear focus needs to be on their own individual strengths,” he said.“It's almost the coaches and the support staff's role to put them into the positions where they're likely to have the most success rather than them having to think too much about whether they need to adapt. It's actually us taking that pressure on ourselves to put them in the positions where they're most successful.”Williams is keen to use the available information without complicating decisions for players in the middle.“I'm someone that I do like the data and analytics side of cricket, but also very mindful that it's still a game. You don't want to be complicating and it's a really hard game to play. So, certainly want the players to be really focused on just what their task is at that moment and not be worrying too much about numbers and all that sort of stuff because it's a hard enough game without a lot of the stuff,” he said.Williams has also watched the WPL’s effect on Indian women’s cricket over its four seasons. He pointed to the national team’s World Cup win and the growing willingness of players to take risks.“I'm very excited about Indian women's cricket and the direction that it's heading. Obviously, the WPL, we've had four seasons of it, and in those four years, India have won a World Cup. And so, I certainly think you can sort of see the fruits of the investment in the WPL,” he said.“I think year on year, just the bravery and the way that the players take the game on, the athleticism across all teams and in the field continues to grow and grow every single year. But I think if I was going to pick one thing with the WPL's growth, it's just been that really taking the game on and that bravery to take risks and those sort of things.”As he prepares for his first season in charge of Mumbai, Williams wants the players and staff to take pride in representing the franchise.“I really want the group to love what they're doing, to be so proud of representing MI and we're in such a fortunate position to be able to represent the franchise, to play cricket professionally and really want to inspire the next generation of players in India and hopefully for the Mumbai Indians,” he said.“So, I really want all of our group, whether it's our staff, our players, to be passionate about what they do, love the franchise and really enjoy ourselves because we're very lucky to do what we do.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4, Live Score: India A made a strong comeback in the opening unofficial Test against New Zealand A,
articles.body: India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4 Live Score: Nabi's first wicket 2.1 overs: Tim Robinson given lbw Nabi struck in his first over, trapping Tim Robinson leg-before-wicket for a duck. The delivery was full and moved towards leg-stump as Robinson tried to play a clip shot but missed. The ball hit him high on the pads, and the umpire raised his finger after an appeal. Robinson appeared unhappy with the decision as he walked back to the pavilion. Tim Robinson lbw b Auqib Nabi 0 (5 balls).India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4 Live Score: Auqib Nabi's three-wicket burst puts India A on top Auqib Nabi struck three times early on Day 4 to put New Zealand A under pressure, giving India A a strong start in their bid for victory in the first unofficial Test..India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4, Live Score: Sundar, Nabi extend India's lead India A's lower order continued to add valuable runs even after Rathod's dismissal. Anshul Kamboj scored 22, hitting four boundaries, before getting out. Washington Sundar and Auqib Nabi then added 69 runs to push the visitors further ahead. Nabi contributed 38 before losing his wicket, while Sundar remained unbeaten on 51 when bad light brought an early end to the day's play. New Zealand A also missed the services of injured seamer Simon Keene, who had taken five wickets in India's first innings. Zak Gibson was their most successful bowler on Day 3, finishing with two wickets for 58 runs..India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4, Live Score: Padikkal misses double century by one run Padikkal's outstanding innings came to an end at 199 in a controversial manner. He was given out caught behind down the leg-side, just one run short of a double century. The batter appeared to question the decision, gesturing towards the umpire as he seemed to indicate that there was a gap between his bat and the ball. His dismissal ended a superb innings that had put India A in a strong position after their difficult start to the match..India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4, Live Score: Rathod keeps up the attack Yash Rathod joined Padikkal and ensured that India A did not lose their momentum. He attacked Lennox and also hit Kristian Clarke for two boundaries and a six. Rathod reached his half-century in just 54 balls, supporting Padikkal as India A extended their advantage. He eventually scored 66 before getting out after Tea..India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4, Live Score: Padikkal, Sudharsan turn the game around India A resumed Day 3 at 56, with Padikkal batting alongside Sai Sudharsan, who was unbeaten on 39 overnight. The two left-handers put the New Zealand A bowlers under pressure with positive batting and helped India A move ahead in the match. Sudharsan scored a valuable 91 before New Zealand A dismissed him with a short-ball plan. Padikkal continued to attack and reached his 12th first-class century by hitting Jayden Lennox for a six. The partnership gave India A control of the game. However, Sudharsan's dismissal and the departure of captain Dhruv Jurel briefly gave the hosts a chance to fight back..India A vs New Zealand A 1st Unofficial Test, Day 4, Live Score: Devdutt Padikkal's 199 puts India A in command India A made a strong comeback in the opening unofficial Test against New Zealand A, taking control of the match after overcoming a first-innings deficit. Devdutt Padikkal led the recovery with a brilliant 199 as India A reached 488/8 at stumps on Day 3 in Lincoln on Monday. The visitors now have a lead of 284 runs after New Zealand A scored 317 in their first innings.
